modules.title: Spark loop
modules.skill: modes, whole-frame copying, and readable change
modules.meaning: a registered three-row spark brightens into a wider flare, holds, then settles
modules.first_reading: the core changes from a placeholder point to a dim spark while every ray stays registered
modules.principle: test the smallest readable multi-row subject before adding frames
modules.defect: only the centre glyph changes while the surrounding rays drift or a duplicate has no timing purpose
modules.basic: find and replace one feature inside a readable three-row frame
modules.scaled: duplicate the complete three-row frame before changing only the copy

modules.title: Contour run
modules.skill: glyph geometry, shallow curves, and precise landmarks
modules.meaning: an anchored shallow contour rises and falls without moving its endpoint
modules.first_reading: the uncertain comma joint becomes the chosen colon joint while the contour and anchor stay fixed
modules.principle: reuse one memorised slope vocabulary across every frame
modules.defect: the endpoint or material spelling shifts when only the contour angle should change
modules.basic: reach a visible joint with f and replace only that joint
modules.scaled: use a bounded substitute or dot repeat for the same joint in several complete frames

modules.title: Face focus
modules.skill: operator/motion grammar inside a stable contour
modules.meaning: a four-row face changes focus and blinks while its silhouette stays registered
modules.first_reading: the annotation disappears, but all four rows of the face remain unchanged
modules.principle: make an operator no larger than the facial feature it is meant to change
modules.defect: a command consumes the mouth or contour when only the eye should change
modules.basic: find the eye and replace one glyph with r
modules.scaled: use a narrowly matched substitute only when several frames need the same facial edit

modules.title: Pose copy
modules.skill: duplicate a whole key pose and change one acting feature
modules.meaning: one registered six-row body carries a small eye change across key poses
modules.first_reading: the eye changes from a placeholder to the approved open focus while the six-row body stays fixed
modules.principle: derive every later frame from the approved complete primary pose
modules.defect: only part of the body was copied, or stable torso and feet drift with the eye
modules.basic: copy all six pose rows with 6yy/p, then edit only the copy
modules.scaled: copy the addressed six-line pose with :t, then change one acting feature

modules.title: Rotation tween
modules.skill: multi-row extremes, midpoint, and stable pivot
modules.meaning: a two-cell prop rotates around a registered body pivot through a vertical midpoint
modules.first_reading: only the copied prop turns from backslashes to forward slashes around the same pivot
modules.principle: draw both complete extremes before inserting the middle in-between
modules.defect: the body pivot or baseline drifts while only the two prop cells should rotate
modules.basic: replace the moving prop cells while preserving the pivot row
modules.scaled: use visual block only for a true aligned prop column inside complete frames

modules.title: Layered scene
modules.meaning: a swinging foreground blade stays separate from a textured background in every frame
modules.first_reading: one covered background stroke is erased so it no longer joins the foreground pivot
modules.principle: erase from the background layer at every false seam while preserving the foreground silhouette
modules.defect: a background stroke touches the pivot and makes the blade and ground read as one object
modules.basic: erase one covered background cell in the complete layered frame
modules.scaled: copy the entire seven-row layered frame before moving the foreground and its background hole

modules.title: Pyramid build
modules.meaning: a five-row finished form is deconstructed without changing frame height, then reordered for forward playback
modules.first_reading: the placeholder apex becomes the finished keyframe apex without changing the other four rows
modules.principle: author an accretive effect backward from its finished keyframe while preserving equal frame bounds
modules.defect: authoring order is mistaken for playback order or deletion collapses a frame's height
modules.basic: copy a complete frame, then blank one unit without deleting its row
modules.scaled: copy or move exact five-line frame ranges with :t and :m

modules.title: Timed build
modules.skill: holds, dot repeat, macro, and scoped polish
modules.meaning: the five-row build pauses before completion and removes an accidental trailing duplicate
modules.first_reading: a complete five-row incomplete build is repeated before completion to create anticipation
modules.principle: a hold repeats a complete frame for a declared timing reason
modules.defect: an identical frame is added without a timing role or a range edit leaks into the completed pose
modules.basic: repeat one bounded feature change in the matching held frame with dot
modules.scaled: record a frame-local substitution as a macro or use an exact frame range

modules.title: Walk study
modules.skill: contact, secondary motion, and equal frame height
modules.meaning: a four-frame five-row walker plants alternating feet while its raised arm lags the body
modules.first_reading: the leading foot gains a ground-contact mark while the torso and raised arm stay registered
modules.principle: track the planted contact cell and let the secondary arm arrive on a different frame
modules.defect: the planted foot slides, the torso shifts, or the arm flips without an adjacent transition
modules.basic: change only the moving foot or arm inside a copied complete pose
modules.scaled: use a bounded pattern or range when the same secondary-motion spelling recurs
modules.source_ref: ascii-art-authoring §§9g-10; walk timing 4+4+2 as method reference

modules.title: Original bounce capstone
modules.skill: plan, keyframe, tween, preview, and revise
modules.meaning: an original three-row ball falls, squashes on a registered ground, rebounds with overshoot, then settles through the loop seam
modules.first_reading: the planned high keyframe replaces its placeholder while the ground row remains registered
modules.principle: state the motion, frame size, extremes, timing, and ground anchor before inserting the falling midpoint
modules.defect: a recycled subject or unplanned middle pose is mistaken for original keyframe authoring
modules.basic: author one readable high extreme and one squash extreme inside equal three-row bounds
modules.scaled: copy complete frames, insert the fall midpoint, preview squash and rebound, then revise the seam

modules.title: SJIS puff tween
modules.skill: proportional contour motion, occlusion stacks, bounded hatching, and true-metric review
modules.meaning: a three-row proportional puff expands from a lobe into an arch, holds at impact with bounded hatching, then settles
modules.first_reading: the missing partner becomes ⌒ヽ while the lower two contour rows remain registered
modules.principle: keep complete equal-height frames and stable contour landmarks, but judge proportional alignment in Saitamaar at true advances
modules.defect: a shoulder changes without its lower contour, hatching escapes the outline, or terminal-cell alignment is mistaken for proportional visual evidence
modules.basic: edit one measured pair inside a complete three-row puff frame and preserve the other contour rows
modules.scaled: copy the complete three-row frame, transform its outline as one pose, and preview the ordered strip in Saitamaar

modules.title: Fixed-width redraw
modules.skill: replace-mode redraw, meaningful undo/redo, and virtual-column motion blur
modules.meaning: a paired three-row machinery loop changes surface tension in place, proves recovery, and adds aligned motion-blur trails past short rows
modules.first_reading: the first roof changes from a loose -- band to a taut == band without shifting either side wall
modules.principle: overwrite fixed-width art when the row length must remain stable, and use virtual columns only when the intended glyph lies beyond end-of-line
modules.defect: inserted or deleted cells shift the machinery walls, undo/redo is performed as a no-op demonstration, or blur trails land in different columns
modules.basic: redraw a bounded run with Replace mode while preserving both endpoints
modules.scaled: recover and reapply a real redraw, compare Replace with Visual replacement, then place homologous trails at one virtual column
modules.source_ref: ascii-art-authoring §§4.4,9h-10; Neovim help R, undo-redo, virtualedit, bar

modules.title: Joint sweep
modules.skill: staggered bilateral accents with till motions and repeated character searches
modules.meaning: a three-row mirrored mechanism passes a joint accent from left to right, then staggers the lower joints before returning on the opposite side
modules.first_reading: the left upper joint changes from : to ! while the centre axis, mirrored outline, and right joint stay registered
modules.principle: preserve the already paired shell and centre axis while addressing homologous punctuation by its visible landmark rather than memorised columns
modules.defect: the stable shell is reversed unnecessarily, a character search lands on the delimiter instead of beside it, or both joint accents change at the same time despite a planned stagger
modules.basic: use t or T to approach a visible joint from either direction, then make one in-place replacement
modules.scaled: repeat a character search across homologous joints, compare it with a row-scoped substitute, and author the mirrored return pose
modules.source_ref: ascii-art-authoring §10 stagger and drag; Neovim help f, t, ;, comma

modules.title: Texture pulse
modules.skill: WORD landmarks across separated texture clusters and a travelling material accent
modules.meaning: an accent travels from the centre texture cluster to the right, expands to three cluster edges, flashes, then exits left while the support rows stay registered
modules.first_reading: the first cell of the centre punctuation cluster changes from . to ! while all three cluster widths and both support rows remain fixed
modules.principle: treat whitespace-separated texture clusters as WORD landmarks, but replace cells in place so the animation does not collapse its fixed-width layout
modules.defect: a lowercase word motion stops inside punctuation, a delete shifts every later cluster, or the pulse changes support rows that should remain temporal anchors
modules.basic: use W to reach the next punctuation cluster and replace its first cell without changing row length
modules.scaled: combine E, counted W, and B to address opposite cluster edges, then compare local repeated edits with a row-scoped material substitution
modules.source_ref: ascii-art-authoring §§5,10; Neovim help WORD, W, B, E

modules.title: Variant palette
modules.skill: paragraph frame objects, named glyph registers, and non-shifting palette replacement
modules.meaning: three blank-line-separated face variants keep one silhouette while their registered eye glyph changes from the saved palette
modules.first_reading: the first face keeps its three-row outline while only its eye changes from o to the palette glyph *
modules.principle: keep variants in the file, treat each blank-line-separated frame as one object, and reuse a deliberate glyph vocabulary instead of retyping it from memory
modules.defect: a put copies only one row, a register paste inserts and shifts the right wall, or a palette glyph is retyped inconsistently between variants
modules.basic: yank one visible palette glyph into a named register and insert it through Replace mode over the acting cell
modules.scaled: copy an entire paragraph frame with yap, navigate variants with }, and compare objectwise put with an addressed range copy
modules.source_ref: ascii-art-authoring §§1.7,2,3; Neovim help text-objects, quote_alpha, i_CTRL-R, virtual-replace-mode

modules.title: Texture ground
modules.skill: dither, offset brick, isometric ground shadow, one-cell indentation, block edges, range edits, and reusable macros
modules.meaning: a three-frame ground treatment pans its brick layer, lightens its dither, gains an occluding edge, and settles without moving the angled shadow base
modules.first_reading: the brick row shifts exactly one cell while the dither and angled ground-shadow row remain registered
modules.principle: texture is a material system: offset repeated motifs by measured cells, lighten dither by erasing density, and keep the shadow or isometric base as a stable depth cue
modules.defect: the brick offset is more than one cell, a block append pads or misses a selected row, a broad substitute changes the shadow, or a macro alters support glyphs outside the acting texture row
modules.basic: set one-cell indentation explicitly and shift only the brick material row
modules.scaled: compare a blockwise end append with a bounded range substitute, then record and replay one landmark replacement across repeated dither cells
modules.source_ref: ascii-art-authoring §§3,4,6,8; Neovim help shiftwidth, >>, visual-block, v_b_A, :substitute, q, @

modules.title: Key-pose plan
modules.skill: reference intake, size tests, written frame plans, saved-plate import, addressed copy/move, and numeric frame labels
modules.meaning: one approved small key pose becomes a written multi-block plan whose frame numbers can be copied, incremented, and reordered without retyping the art
modules.first_reading: the small three-row pose is already readable at playback size, while its F01 and T08 FPS lines state frame identity and timing before in-betweening begins
modules.principle: collect a reference, test the smallest readable key pose, write timing and frame intent down, then preserve that approved plate while planning later poses
modules.defect: a copied plan block loses an art row, two blocks retain the same frame number, a move cuts through a five-line plate, or an imported plate comes from unsaved buffer state instead of the named source
modules.basic: increment a numeric frame label in place with CTRL-A while the pose and timing line remain unchanged
modules.scaled: read a saved plate, copy complete five-line plan blocks by address, and compare addressed move with a linewise delete-and-put reorder
modules.source_ref: ascii-art-authoring §§2,7.1; archived animation workflow transcript Part 1 00:52:45–01:01:05; Neovim help :read, :copy, :move, CTRL-A

modules.title: Coherent anchors
modules.skill: unchanged-glyph coherence across frames with search repeat, dot repeat, :global normal, and recorded macros
modules.meaning: four changing shell poses keep one eye material coherent until an intentional strip-wide palette pass changes that homologous cell in every frame
modules.first_reading: the shells change pose while the eye is the same semantic anchor in every frame; the first pass corrects only those homologous eye cells
modules.principle: unchanged glyphs are temporal anchors: batch-edit only a proven homologous landmark, then inspect every frame for collateral changes before playback
modules.defect: one frame keeps the old eye, a repeat lands on contour punctuation, :global selects an unrelated line, or a macro wraps beyond the owned landmark count
modules.basic: replace the first searched eye and use n plus dot to repeat the exact edit at the next frame landmarks
modules.scaled: compare search-and-dot with :global normal, then record a search-bearing macro and replay it across a known number of frame anchors

modules.title: Hand-mirrored return
modules.skill: full directional hand mirrors, validation-only expression substitution, and reverse-order frame reuse
modules.meaning: a right-facing action is redrawn by hand as a left-facing return, checked without generating art, eased into an overshoot, and reused in reverse around an intentional turnaround hold
modules.first_reading: the actor, arrowhead, slash limbs, and whitespace all exchange direction by authored judgment while the frame width and rails remain fixed
modules.principle: never reverse stored bytes to mirror ASCII art; redraw directional glyphs and spacing by eye, validate the result separately, then reuse approved frames in reverse when the motion physically returns
modules.defect: a slash points inward after mirroring, the actor shifts to the wrong distance from the rail, an expression replacement generates the art instead of only checking it, or reverse reuse adds an unexplained duplicate
modules.basic: overwrite all three art rows with a deliberate hand-authored mirror while leaving the validation line pending
modules.scaled: compare manual validation with a check-only \= expression, then append approved frame ranges in reverse order with an explicit turnaround hold

legacy_lessons.title: raise the joint
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Motions: moving the cursor IS editing
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
In most editors, moving the cursor and changing the text are two different
activities. You arrow over to a spot, then you do a thing. In vim the motion is
an ingredient of the change, so the two collapse into one thought.

  f,     move to the next comma
  df,    delete up to and including the next comma
  ct,    change everything up to but not including the next comma

`df,` is not three keystrokes that happen to be adjacent. It is one intention.
This is why counting keystrokes is the wrong scorecard. The right question is
how many DECISIONS an edit took, and the answer should usually be one.

  f{char}  find the next one on this line      F{char}  find the previous one
  t{char}  stop just before the next one       T{char}  stop just after the previous
  ;        do that find again                  ,        do it backwards
  0 ^ $    start of line, first real char, end of line
  %        bounce between matching brackets    }        next blank line

Precision beats speed. h and l are for adjusting by one cell, not for travelling.
If you are pressing l more than about three times, there was a motion for it.
keys: r<char>  replace one character, staying in normal mode
3rx      replace the next three          R  overwrite until <Esc>
legacy_lessons.buys: One glyph, one key, no mode change.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §4.6 rule 5: a joint glyph sits differently in its cell. `.` sits too low, `'` sits too high, `:` sits in the middle.

legacy_lessons.title: stamp a spark
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Lines and blocks: the buffer is two-dimensional
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Most text tooling treats a file as one long string with newlines in it. Vim
treats it as a grid, and gives you operators for both axes.

Along the vertical axis, the line operators:

  dd  delete a line     yy  copy a line      p / P  put it back below / above
  3yy 2p                copy three lines, stamp them down twice
  ddp                   swap this line with the one below it
  :t.  :m0              copy this line to here, move this line to there

Along the horizontal axis, blockwise visual mode:

  <C-v>   select a RECTANGLE, not a run of text
  <C-v>jjI|<Esc>   insert a column down three lines at once
  <C-v>jjd         delete a column
  <C-v>jj$A;<Esc>  append to the end of several lines at once

This is the mode that makes monospaced art tractable. An animation file is a
stack of frames; a frame is a rectangle. Copying a frame, erasing one column
across it, or re-sorting frames into playback order are all one-command
operations here, and they are miserable everywhere else.

Gabriel Santos animates Stone Story RPG in a plain text editor for exactly this
reason: the frames are text, so the text editor is the animation tool.
keys: yy  yank a line    p  put below    P  put above    3p  put three copies
legacy_lessons.buys: Copy and paste, without a clipboard or a mouse.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 1

legacy_lessons.title: swap one glyph
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Ranges and registers: where the editor becomes a small language
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Press `:` and you are no longer pressing keys at an editor, you are issuing
statements to it. Every statement takes a range, and the range is the powerful
half.

  :t.        copy this line to just after this line
  :5,10m0    move lines 5 to 10 to the top of the file
  :%s/o/0/g  substitute across every line in the buffer
  :'<,'>!sort  pipe the visual selection through an external program
  :g/^$/d    run a command on every line matching a pattern

And the yank you did three edits ago is not gone. Vim has a bank of named
clipboards:

  "ayy   yank this line into register a       "ap   put register a back
  "0p    the last yank, even after a delete overwrote the unnamed register
  qa...q record keystrokes into register a, and @a replays them

The macros and the registers are the same storage. A recorded macro is literally
just text in a register, which means you can paste it out, edit it as text, and
yank it back in. That is the point at which the editor stops being a keyboard
game and starts being programmable.
keys: :s/old/new/     first match on this line
:s/old/new/g    every match on this line
:%s/old/new/g   every match in the file
In a pattern, . means any character. Escape it as \. to mean a literal dot.
legacy_lessons.buys: The first taste of the colon line, and of patterns.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §4.6 rule 5: `:` sits at mid-height in the cell, `.` sits too low.

legacy_lessons.title: find the anchor
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Motions: moving the cursor IS editing
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
In most editors, moving the cursor and changing the text are two different
activities. You arrow over to a spot, then you do a thing. In vim the motion is
an ingredient of the change, so the two collapse into one thought.

  f,     move to the next comma
  df,    delete up to and including the next comma
  ct,    change everything up to but not including the next comma

`df,` is not three keystrokes that happen to be adjacent. It is one intention.
This is why counting keystrokes is the wrong scorecard. The right question is
how many DECISIONS an edit took, and the answer should usually be one.

  f{char}  find the next one on this line      F{char}  find the previous one
  t{char}  stop just before the next one       T{char}  stop just after the previous
  ;        do that find again                  ,        do it backwards
  0 ^ $    start of line, first real char, end of line
  %        bounce between matching brackets    }        next blank line

Precision beats speed. h and l are for adjusting by one cell, not for travelling.
If you are pressing l more than about three times, there was a motion for it.
keys: /text  search forward    ?text  search backward
n      next match        N      previous match
<C-o>  jump back to where you were      <C-i>  jump forward again
legacy_lessons.buys: Finding a cell by what is in it, not by counting to it.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 05 section 10, the dithered sphere, lower band

legacy_lessons.title: trim the alphabet
legacy_lessons.concept_title: The grammar: vim is a language, not a list of shortcuts
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
The single idea that turns vim from a chore into a tool: commands are sentences.

  [count]  [operator]  [motion or text object]
   adverb     verb          noun

  d        w                 delete one word
  2 d      w                 delete two words
  c        i(                change what is inside the parentheses
  y        ap                yank around this paragraph
  >        }                 indent to the end of the paragraph

You do not memorise commands. You memorise a small vocabulary of verbs and a
small vocabulary of nouns, and the editor multiplies them for you. Ten verbs and
thirty nouns is three hundred edits you were never explicitly taught, and you
can guess every one of them.

This is why nobody has to tell you what `yi(` does once you know `ci(`. It is
also why `d` alone does nothing: a verb with no object is not a sentence. The
editor is waiting for the rest of it.

  verbs   c change   d delete   y yank   > indent   gu lowercase   = format
  nouns   w word   $ end of line   } paragraph   f. up to a dot   i( inside parens

When you catch yourself pressing x fifteen times, stop. That is not a sentence,
that is a stutter. Find the noun that names what you actually want to remove.
keys: dw   delete a word        de   delete to the end of the word
d$   delete to end of line   dd   delete the line
legacy_lessons.buys: The first verb+noun sentence: delete, a word.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 03 section 5, the four extended glyphs

legacy_lessons.title: check the pair
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Text objects: address the thing, not the coordinates
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Motions move from where you are to somewhere else, so they depend on where you
happen to be standing. Text objects do not. They name a STRUCTURE, and they work
from anywhere inside it.

  iw  the word            aw  the word plus its trailing space
  i(  inside the parens   a(  the parens as well
  i"  inside the quotes   a"  the quotes as well
  ip  this paragraph      ap  the paragraph plus its blank line
  it  inside the XML tag  at  the tag as well

`ci(` means "change what is inside these parentheses" and the cursor can be on
the opening bracket, the closing bracket, or anywhere in between. You do not have
to navigate to an edge first. You do not have to count characters.

This is the difference between an edit that is robust and an edit that is a
stunt. Position-based edits break the moment the text shifts by one character.
Structure-based edits do not, which is also why they survive being recorded into
a macro and replayed across forty lines.

i = inner (the contents). a = around (the contents plus the delimiters). That is
the whole mnemonic, and it composes with every verb you already know.
keys: %    jump between matching ( ) [ ] { }
ci(  change inside parens     ca(  change the parens as well
The cursor may sit anywhere inside the object.
legacy_lessons.buys: i = inner, a = around. One mnemonic, a hundred commands.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 03, Line style This is the lamp's body row.

legacy_lessons.title: stair-step run
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Modes: why the editor has more than one rulebook
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Every other editor you have used runs in one mode. Every key you press inserts
itself, so every COMMAND has to be smuggled in behind a modifier: Ctrl, Cmd,
Alt, or a menu. That single decision is why those editors need a mouse, and why
your hands leave the home row a hundred times an hour.

Vim makes the opposite trade. It splits editing into modes, and each mode is a
small self-contained module with its own rulebook. In Normal mode the entire
alphabet is free, so commands get to be single letters. In Insert mode the
alphabet means letters again. Nothing has to be smuggled.

  Normal   navigate and operate on text          <Esc>
  Insert   type text like a normal editor        i a o I A O
  Visual   select first, then act                v V <C-v>
  Command  talk to the editor in its own line    :

The cost is real: you have to know which mode you are in, and beginners pay for

legacy_lessons.title: around versus inside
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Text objects: address the thing, not the coordinates
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Motions move from where you are to somewhere else, so they depend on where you
happen to be standing. Text objects do not. They name a STRUCTURE, and they work
from anywhere inside it.

  iw  the word            aw  the word plus its trailing space
  i(  inside the parens   a(  the parens as well
  i"  inside the quotes   a"  the quotes as well
  ip  this paragraph      ap  the paragraph plus its blank line
  it  inside the XML tag  at  the tag as well

`ci(` means "change what is inside these parentheses" and the cursor can be on
the opening bracket, the closing bracket, or anywhere in between. You do not have
to navigate to an edge first. You do not have to count characters.

This is the difference between an edit that is robust and an edit that is a
stunt. Position-based edits break the moment the text shifts by one character.
Structure-based edits do not, which is also why they survive being recorded into
a macro and replayed across forty lines.

i = inner (the contents). a = around (the contents plus the delimiters). That is
the whole mnemonic, and it composes with every verb you already know.
keys: ci(  change inside the parens       ca(  change the parens as well
di"  delete inside quotes           dap  delete a paragraph and its blank line
i = inner, a = around.
legacy_lessons.buys: The difference between the contents and the container.

legacy_lessons.title: two glyphs at once
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Ranges and registers: where the editor becomes a small language
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Press `:` and you are no longer pressing keys at an editor, you are issuing
statements to it. Every statement takes a range, and the range is the powerful
half.

  :t.        copy this line to just after this line
  :5,10m0    move lines 5 to 10 to the top of the file
  :%s/o/0/g  substitute across every line in the buffer
  :'<,'>!sort  pipe the visual selection through an external program
  :g/^$/d    run a command on every line matching a pattern

And the yank you did three edits ago is not gone. Vim has a bank of named
clipboards:

  "ayy   yank this line into register a       "ap   put register a back
  "0p    the last yank, even after a delete overwrote the unnamed register
  qa...q record keystrokes into register a, and @a replays them

The macros and the registers are the same storage. A recorded macro is literally
just text in a register, which means you can paste it out, edit it as text, and
yank it back in. That is the point at which the editor stops being a keyboard
game and starts being programmable.
keys: "ayy  yank a line into register a      "ap  put it back
"Ayy  APPEND to register a             :reg  list every register
Twenty-six registers means twenty-six glyphs held at once.
legacy_lessons.buys: A bank of clipboards, which is what glyph work actually needs.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §1.7: keep a symbol-table file of glyphs open beside the drawing. Named registers are that table, inside the editor.

legacy_lessons.title: shallowest gradient
legacy_lessons.concept_title: The grammar: vim is a language, not a list of shortcuts
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
The single idea that turns vim from a chore into a tool: commands are sentences.

  [count]  [operator]  [motion or text object]
   adverb     verb          noun

  d        w                 delete one word
  2 d      w                 delete two words
  c        i(                change what is inside the parentheses
  y        ap                yank around this paragraph
  >        }                 indent to the end of the paragraph

You do not memorise commands. You memorise a small vocabulary of verbs and a
small vocabulary of nouns, and the editor multiplies them for you. Ten verbs and
thirty nouns is three hundred edits you were never explicitly taught, and you
can guess every one of them.

This is why nobody has to tell you what `yi(` does once you know `ci(`. It is
also why `d` alone does nothing: a verb with no object is not a sentence. The
editor is waiting for the rest of it.

  verbs   c change   d delete   y yank   > indent   gu lowercase   = format
  nouns   w word   $ end of line   } paragraph   f. up to a dot   i( inside parens

When you catch yourself pressing x fifteen times, stop. That is not a sentence,
that is a stutter. Find the noun that names what you actually want to remove.
keys: C = c$  change to end of line      A  append at end of line
0  start of line   ^  first non-blank   $  end of line
ZZ save and quit                   ZQ quit without saving
legacy_lessons.buys: The shorthand verbs: each is a contraction of a whole sentence.

legacy_lessons.title: break the seam
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Text objects: address the thing, not the coordinates
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Motions move from where you are to somewhere else, so they depend on where you
happen to be standing. Text objects do not. They name a STRUCTURE, and they work
from anywhere inside it.

  iw  the word            aw  the word plus its trailing space
  i(  inside the parens   a(  the parens as well
  i"  inside the quotes   a"  the quotes as well
  ip  this paragraph      ap  the paragraph plus its blank line
  it  inside the XML tag  at  the tag as well

`ci(` means "change what is inside these parentheses" and the cursor can be on
the opening bracket, the closing bracket, or anywhere in between. You do not have
to navigate to an edge first. You do not have to count characters.

This is the difference between an edit that is robust and an edit that is a
stunt. Position-based edits break the moment the text shifts by one character.
Structure-based edits do not, which is also why they survive being recorded into
a macro and replayed across forty lines.

i = inner (the contents). a = around (the contents plus the delimiters). That is
the whole mnemonic, and it composes with every verb you already know.
keys: The plate shows this edit as a before/after pair, with an arrow between them.
It is two character replacements, and it is the whole depth technique:
a shared glyph reads as a join           break it
a deleted cell at a seam reads as shadow leave it empty
legacy_lessons.buys: Depth, from one character. This is the highest-value edit in the whole method.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 05 section 9, two forms sharing a seam glyph skill §3: a glyph shared between two objects creates a false connection. Replace it with a partial-coverage glyph placed away from the seam.

legacy_lessons.title: duplicate a base row
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Ranges and registers: where the editor becomes a small language
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Press `:` and you are no longer pressing keys at an editor, you are issuing
statements to it. Every statement takes a range, and the range is the powerful
half.

  :t.        copy this line to just after this line
  :5,10m0    move lines 5 to 10 to the top of the file
  :%s/o/0/g  substitute across every line in the buffer
  :'<,'>!sort  pipe the visual selection through an external program
  :g/^$/d    run a command on every line matching a pattern

And the yank you did three edits ago is not gone. Vim has a bank of named
clipboards:

  "ayy   yank this line into register a       "ap   put register a back
  "0p    the last yank, even after a delete overwrote the unnamed register
  qa...q record keystrokes into register a, and @a replays them

The macros and the registers are the same storage. A recorded macro is literally
just text in a register, which means you can paste it out, edit it as text, and
yank it back in. That is the point at which the editor stops being a keyboard
game and starts being programmable.
keys: :t.   copy this line below itself     :t0  copy it to the top
:m0   move this line to the top       :m$  move it to the bottom
yyp does the same as :t. Ranges scale to a hundred lines; yyp does not.
legacy_lessons.buys: The colon line takes a range, and the range is the half that scales.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06 section 13, subtractive-animation pyramid, frame 1 of 7 The base rows of the pyramid.

legacy_lessons.title: close the seam
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Lines and blocks: the buffer is two-dimensional
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Most text tooling treats a file as one long string with newlines in it. Vim
treats it as a grid, and gives you operators for both axes.

Along the vertical axis, the line operators:

  dd  delete a line     yy  copy a line      p / P  put it back below / above
  3yy 2p                copy three lines, stamp them down twice
  ddp                   swap this line with the one below it
  :t.  :m0              copy this line to here, move this line to there

Along the horizontal axis, blockwise visual mode:

  <C-v>   select a RECTANGLE, not a run of text
  <C-v>jjI|<Esc>   insert a column down three lines at once
  <C-v>jjd         delete a column
  <C-v>jj$A;<Esc>  append to the end of several lines at once

This is the mode that makes monospaced art tractable. An animation file is a
stack of frames; a frame is a rectangle. Copying a frame, erasing one column
across it, or re-sorting frames into playback order are all one-command
operations here, and they are miserable everywhere else.

Gabriel Santos animates Stone Story RPG in a plain text editor for exactly this
reason: the frames are text, so the text editor is the animation tool.
keys: J   join the line below, inserting a space
gJ  join without inserting anything
3J  join three lines
legacy_lessons.buys: Two rows become one row without retyping either.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §4.7 drill 2: type the run, then type it mirrored.

legacy_lessons.title: cut the label
legacy_lessons.concept_title: The grammar: vim is a language, not a list of shortcuts
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
The single idea that turns vim from a chore into a tool: commands are sentences.

  [count]  [operator]  [motion or text object]
   adverb     verb          noun

  d        w                 delete one word
  2 d      w                 delete two words
  c        i(                change what is inside the parentheses
  y        ap                yank around this paragraph
  >        }                 indent to the end of the paragraph

You do not memorise commands. You memorise a small vocabulary of verbs and a
small vocabulary of nouns, and the editor multiplies them for you. Ten verbs and
thirty nouns is three hundred edits you were never explicitly taught, and you
can guess every one of them.

This is why nobody has to tell you what `yi(` does once you know `ci(`. It is
also why `d` alone does nothing: a verb with no object is not a sentence. The
editor is waiting for the rest of it.

  verbs   c change   d delete   y yank   > indent   gu lowercase   = format
  nouns   w word   $ end of line   } paragraph   f. up to a dot   i( inside parens

When you catch yourself pressing x fifteen times, stop. That is not a sentence,
that is a stutter. Find the noun that names what you actually want to remove.
keys: D = d$   delete to end of line      C = c$   change to end of line
F<char>  find backwards on this line
legacy_lessons.buys: Stripping a label off a line without counting characters.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 03, Line style The plate labels the style beside the art.

legacy_lessons.title: walk an edit down
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Repetition: fast editing is repeatable editing, not fast typing
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Watching an expert use vim, the obvious conclusion is that they type quickly.
They do not. What they do is structure each edit so that the editor can perform
it again for them.

Vim gives you three tiers of replay, and they cover almost everything:

  .        repeat the last change, once, wherever the cursor now is
  3a-<Esc> do the insert three times as a single change
  qq ... q record a macro, then @q replays it, 10@q replays it ten times
  :%s///   apply one substitution to every line at once

This has a consequence that is easy to miss: a sloppy edit is a dead end and a
precise edit is an asset. If you fix a line with five improvised keystrokes,
nothing can replay that. If you fix it with `ciw` plus a word, `.` will fix the
next nine occurrences for free. The habit is to make edits small, named, and
repeatable, and then let the editor do the volume.

It is also why `u` (undo) is cheap here. Try a repeatable edit, watch it apply,
undo it if it was wrong. The cost of a wrong guess is one keystroke.
keys: j keeps your column, so j. walks one edit down a stack of frames
3.  repeat the change three times
For a taller stack, record it: qq r: j q  then 20@q
legacy_lessons.buys: Vertical repetition without a macro.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §4.6 rule 5: `.` sits too low, `'` too high, `:` in the middle.

legacy_lessons.title: lighten every band
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Ranges and registers: where the editor becomes a small language
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Press `:` and you are no longer pressing keys at an editor, you are issuing
statements to it. Every statement takes a range, and the range is the powerful
half.

  :t.        copy this line to just after this line
  :5,10m0    move lines 5 to 10 to the top of the file
  :%s/o/0/g  substitute across every line in the buffer
  :'<,'>!sort  pipe the visual selection through an external program
  :g/^$/d    run a command on every line matching a pattern

And the yank you did three edits ago is not gone. Vim has a bank of named
clipboards:

  "ayy   yank this line into register a       "ap   put register a back
  "0p    the last yank, even after a delete overwrote the unnamed register
  qa...q record keystrokes into register a, and @a replays them

The macros and the registers are the same storage. A recorded macro is literally
just text in a register, which means you can paste it out, edit it as text, and
yank it back in. That is the point at which the editor stops being a keyboard
game and starts being programmable.
keys: :%s/a/b/g    every match in the file
:%s/a/b/gc   ask for confirmation at each one
:5,9s/a/b/g  only on lines 5 to 9
legacy_lessons.buys: One command instead of forty edits.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §8 rule 2: lighten a shading band by erasing members of it, not by swapping to a lighter glyph.

legacy_lessons.title: hop the band
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Motions: moving the cursor IS editing
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
In most editors, moving the cursor and changing the text are two different
activities. You arrow over to a spot, then you do a thing. In vim the motion is
an ingredient of the change, so the two collapse into one thought.

  f,     move to the next comma
  df,    delete up to and including the next comma
  ct,    change everything up to but not including the next comma

`df,` is not three keystrokes that happen to be adjacent. It is one intention.
This is why counting keystrokes is the wrong scorecard. The right question is
how many DECISIONS an edit took, and the answer should usually be one.

  f{char}  find the next one on this line      F{char}  find the previous one
  t{char}  stop just before the next one       T{char}  stop just after the previous
  ;        do that find again                  ,        do it backwards
  0 ^ $    start of line, first real char, end of line
  %        bounce between matching brackets    }        next blank line

Precision beats speed. h and l are for adjusting by one cell, not for travelling.
If you are pressing l more than about three times, there was a motion for it.
keys: f:  find next :     F:  find previous :     ;  repeat     ,  reverse
t:  stop just BEFORE the next :            df:  delete up to and including it
legacy_lessons.buys: Travelling by landmark instead of counting cells.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §8: a shading band alternates two glyphs, which makes it a row of landmarks.

legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Most text tooling treats a file as one long string with newlines in it. Vim
treats it as a grid, and gives you operators for both axes.

Along the vertical axis, the line operators:

  dd  delete a line     yy  copy a line      p / P  put it back below / above
  3yy 2p                copy three lines, stamp them down twice
  ddp                   swap this line with the one below it
  :t.  :m0              copy this line to here, move this line to there

Along the horizontal axis, blockwise visual mode:

  <C-v>   select a RECTANGLE, not a run of text
  <C-v>jjI|<Esc>   insert a column down three lines at once
  <C-v>jjd         delete a column
  <C-v>jj$A;<Esc>  append to the end of several lines at once

This is the mode that makes monospaced art tractable. An animation file is a
stack of frames; a frame is a rectangle. Copying a frame, erasing one column
across it, or re-sorting frames into playback order are all one-command
operations here, and they are miserable everywhere else.

Gabriel Santos animates Stone Story RPG in a plain text editor for exactly this
reason: the frames are text, so the text editor is the animation tool.
keys: o  open a line below and start typing      O  open one above
Frames in a set must be the same height, so padding is routine.
legacy_lessons.buys: Padding frames to a common height, one keystroke per row.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 1 skill §9 step h: pad every frame to the height of the tallest one before rendering.

legacy_lessons.title: ground the run
legacy_lessons.concept_title: The grammar: vim is a language, not a list of shortcuts
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
The single idea that turns vim from a chore into a tool: commands are sentences.

  [count]  [operator]  [motion or text object]
   adverb     verb          noun

  d        w                 delete one word
  2 d      w                 delete two words
  c        i(                change what is inside the parentheses
  y        ap                yank around this paragraph
  >        }                 indent to the end of the paragraph

You do not memorise commands. You memorise a small vocabulary of verbs and a
small vocabulary of nouns, and the editor multiplies them for you. Ten verbs and
thirty nouns is three hundred edits you were never explicitly taught, and you
can guess every one of them.

This is why nobody has to tell you what `yi(` does once you know `ci(`. It is
also why `d` alone does nothing: a verb with no object is not a sentence. The
editor is waiting for the rest of it.

  verbs   c change   d delete   y yank   > indent   gu lowercase   = format
  nouns   w word   $ end of line   } paragraph   f. up to a dot   i( inside parens

When you catch yourself pressing x fifteen times, stop. That is not a sentence,
that is a stutter. Find the noun that names what you actually want to remove.
keys: a  append after the cursor      A  append at end of line
i  insert before the cursor     I  insert before the first non-blank
legacy_lessons.buys: Four ways into insert mode, each saving a motion.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §4.4: the classic stair-step is `_ . - ´`. If your keyboard cannot type ´ directly, do the `symbol table` drill instead.

legacy_lessons.title: spark, one cell
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Modes: why the editor has more than one rulebook
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Every other editor you have used runs in one mode. Every key you press inserts
itself, so every COMMAND has to be smuggled in behind a modifier: Ctrl, Cmd,
Alt, or a menu. That single decision is why those editors need a mouse, and why
your hands leave the home row a hundred times an hour.

Vim makes the opposite trade. It splits editing into modes, and each mode is a
small self-contained module with its own rulebook. In Normal mode the entire
alphabet is free, so commands get to be single letters. In Insert mode the
alphabet means letters again. Nothing has to be smuggled.

  Normal   navigate and operate on text          <Esc>
  Insert   type text like a normal editor        i a o I A O
  Visual   select first, then act                v V <C-v>
  Command  talk to the editor in its own line    :

The cost is real: you have to know which mode you are in, and beginners pay for
that in confusion. The payoff is that commands become composable letters instead
of chords, and composable letters can be multiplied together. That multiplication
is the whole reason the rest of these drills exist.

Practical rule: Normal mode is home. You visit Insert mode, you do not live
there. If you find yourself holding a key down, you are in the wrong mode.
keys: h j k l   left down up right, without leaving the home row
dd  delete a line     x  delete a character     u  undo
legacy_lessons.buys: The home-row four. Every motion you learn later replaces these.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 4 The particle layer is a one-cell animation.

legacy_lessons.title: delete, then think again
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Repetition: fast editing is repeatable editing, not fast typing
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Watching an expert use vim, the obvious conclusion is that they type quickly.
They do not. What they do is structure each edit so that the editor can perform
it again for them.

Vim gives you three tiers of replay, and they cover almost everything:

  .        repeat the last change, once, wherever the cursor now is
  3a-<Esc> do the insert three times as a single change
  qq ... q record a macro, then @q replays it, 10@q replays it ten times
  :%s///   apply one substitution to every line at once

This has a consequence that is easy to miss: a sloppy edit is a dead end and a
precise edit is an asset. If you fix a line with five improvised keystrokes,
nothing can replay that. If you fix it with `ciw` plus a word, `.` will fix the
next nine occurrences for free. The habit is to make edits small, named, and
repeatable, and then let the editor do the volume.

It is also why `u` (undo) is cheap here. Try a repeatable edit, watch it apply,
undo it if it was wrong. The cost of a wrong guess is one keystroke.
keys: u      undo the last change        <C-r>  redo
U      undo every change on this line
Undo is cheap. That is what makes guessing a command a reasonable move.
legacy_lessons.buys: Nothing you try in normal mode costs more than one keystroke to take back.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06, apex rows of pyramid frames 1 to 5

legacy_lessons.title: the symbol table
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Ranges and registers: where the editor becomes a small language
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Press `:` and you are no longer pressing keys at an editor, you are issuing
statements to it. Every statement takes a range, and the range is the powerful
half.

  :t.        copy this line to just after this line
  :5,10m0    move lines 5 to 10 to the top of the file
  :%s/o/0/g  substitute across every line in the buffer
  :'<,'>!sort  pipe the visual selection through an external program
  :g/^$/d    run a command on every line matching a pattern

And the yank you did three edits ago is not gone. Vim has a bank of named
clipboards:

  "ayy   yank this line into register a       "ap   put register a back
  "0p    the last yank, even after a delete overwrote the unnamed register
  qa...q record keystrokes into register a, and @a replays them

The macros and the registers are the same storage. A recorded macro is literally
just text in a register, which means you can paste it out, edit it as text, and
yank it back in. That is the point at which the editor stops being a keyboard
game and starts being programmable.
keys: yl   yank one character         3yl  yank three
vp   select, then put OVER the selection
This is how an artist types a glyph the keyboard does not have: keep a
strip of them in the file and copy from it. Never retype by hand.
legacy_lessons.buys: The four extended glyphs, without fighting your keyboard layout.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §1.7: keep the glyph alphabet open beside the drawing. skill §4.2: ´ is the mirror of the backtick. It is not the apostrophe, and it is not on your keyboard.

legacy_lessons.title: drop a layer
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Lines and blocks: the buffer is two-dimensional
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Most text tooling treats a file as one long string with newlines in it. Vim
treats it as a grid, and gives you operators for both axes.

Along the vertical axis, the line operators:

  dd  delete a line     yy  copy a line      p / P  put it back below / above
  3yy 2p                copy three lines, stamp them down twice
  ddp                   swap this line with the one below it
  :t.  :m0              copy this line to here, move this line to there

Along the horizontal axis, blockwise visual mode:

  <C-v>   select a RECTANGLE, not a run of text
  <C-v>jjI|<Esc>   insert a column down three lines at once
  <C-v>jjd         delete a column
  <C-v>jj$A;<Esc>  append to the end of several lines at once

This is the mode that makes monospaced art tractable. An animation file is a
stack of frames; a frame is a rectangle. Copying a frame, erasing one column
across it, or re-sorting frames into playback order are all one-command
operations here, and they are miserable everywhere else.

Gabriel Santos animates Stone Story RPG in a plain text editor for exactly this
reason: the frames are text, so the text editor is the animation tool.
keys: dap  delete a paragraph and its blank line    dip  just the paragraph
yap  yank one                                 }    jump to the next blank line
A blank-line-separated block IS a layer. That is why ap matters here.
legacy_lessons.buys: A frame or a layer is a paragraph. Address it as one.
legacy_lessons.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 1 skill §3 rule 5: layers are stored as blank-line-separated blocks in one file, back layer first.

legacy_lessons.title: rotation in-between
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Lines and blocks: the buffer is two-dimensional
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
Most text tooling treats a file as one long string with newlines in it. Vim
treats it as a grid, and gives you operators for both axes.

Along the vertical axis, the line operators:

  dd  delete a line     yy  copy a line      p / P  put it back below / above
  3yy 2p                copy three lines, stamp them down twice
  ddp                   swap this line with the one below it
  :t.  :m0              copy this line to here, move this line to there

Along the horizontal axis, blockwise visual mode:

  <C-v>   select a RECTANGLE, not a run of text
  <C-v>jjI|<Esc>   insert a column down three lines at once
  <C-v>jjd         delete a column
  <C-v>jj$A;<Esc>  append to the end of several lines at once

This is the mode that makes monospaced art tractable. An animation file is a
stack of frames; a frame is a rectangle. Copying a frame, erasing one column
across it, or re-sorting frames into playback order are all one-command
operations here, and they are miserable everywhere else.

Gabriel Santos animates Stone Story RPG in a plain text editor for exactly this
reason: the frames are text, so the text editor is the animation tool.
keys: <C-v>jj$A  appends to lines of different lengths, correctly
<C-v>jjI   inserts at a fixed column instead
legacy_lessons.buys: The in-between frame of a rotation, in one command.
legacy_lessons.source: skill §4.4: `\` then `\|` then `/` is the rotation triple. The bar is the tween.

legacy_lessons.title: hand-mirrored run
legacy_lessons.concept_title: Motions: moving the cursor IS editing
legacy_lessons.paradigm:
In most editors, moving the cursor and changing the text are two different
activities. You arrow over to a spot, then you do a thing. In vim the motion is
an ingredient of the change, so the two collapse into one thought.

  f,     move to the next comma
  df,    delete up to and including the next comma
  ct,    change everything up to but not including the next comma

`df,` is not three keystrokes that happen to be adjacent. It is one intention.
This is why counting keystrokes is the wrong scorecard. The right question is
how many DECISIONS an edit took, and the answer should usually be one.

  f{char}  find the next one on this line      F{char}  find the previous one
  t{char}  stop just before the next one       T{char}  stop just after the previous
  ;        do that find again                  ,        do it backwards
  0 ^ $    start of line, first real char, end of line
  %        bounce between matching brackets    }        next blank line

Precision beats speed. h and l are for adjusting by one cell, not for travelling.
If you are pressing l more than about three times, there was a motion for it.
keys: The mirror table:  _ <-> _    . <-> .    - <-> -
r<char>  replace one character      3rx  replace three
